name: ConvectionKernels (CVTT BC6H decoder)
baseline: bcdec (also AMD Compressonator cmp_core, DirectXTex, SwiftShader, Mesa in the same chart; BC6H unsigned decode only)
workload: Single-thread BC6H (unsigned) texture decode in Mpix/s, from aras-p's June 2022 bcn_decoder_tester harness decoding a set of DDS test images (ambientCG textures, Kodak, Poly Haven HDRI, WebP gallery) with ConvectionKernels ('convection') versus eight other BCn decoders.
claimed_speedup: BC6Hu decode, Mpix/s, labels printed in the chart PNGs (ratios derived from page data): Ryzen 5950X VS2022: convection 101 vs bcdec 85 (1.19x), swiftshader 70, mesa 57, dxtex 25, amd_cmp 9 (11x). Ryzen 5950X clang14: convection 105 vs bcdec 104 (1.01x, a tie), swiftshader 97, mesa 79, dxtex 34, amd_cmp 33 (3.2x). Apple M1 Max clang13: convection 149 vs swiftshader 143 (1.04x), mesa 84, bcdec 79 (1.89x), dxtex 37, amd_cmp 30 (5.0x). Convection is the top BC6H bar in all three charts. On BC7 decode it is slower than bcdec and bc7enc_rdo (VS2022: convection 124 vs bcdec 142 vs bc7dec_rdo 621; M1 Max: 157 vs 220 vs 517).
compiler_and_flags: Chart titles name VS2022, clang14 (Windows) and clang13 (Apple). Public harness aras-p/bcn_decoder_tester builds Windows with CMake preset x64-release = RelWithDebInfo plus /Ob2 (CMakeLists.txt); the macOS build flags are not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5950X (Windows, VS2022 and clang14 charts); Apple M1 Max (macOS clang13 chart); 1 thread
tradeoffs: Stand-alone SPMD-style SIMD kernels extracted from Convection Texture Tools (CVTT); SIMD ops and 16-bit math; the API works on cvtt::NumParallelBlocks blocks at a time, so callers must pad partial batches. README lists BC6H as 'Experimental' and 11-bit EAC as 'Experimental'; BC7, BC1-5 and ETC1/ETC2 as complete; no ASTC or PVRTC. The faster-decode result is for BC6H only.
caveats: The result is about the decoder, not the encoder: the README makes only an unquantified claim ('very high quality at good speed') and no encode comparison against ispc_texcomp, bc7enc or Compressonator was found, so the lead's encoder baselines are untested here. The margin over bcdec is 1% on the clang14 chart and bcdec was an early-2022 snapshot that later moved on (the tester README lists a 2022-09-15 bcdec commit), so a re-run is needed. Per-run flags are inferred from the CMake preset, not printed on the charts; the blog post text was blocked in this environment (aras-p.info EGRESS_BLOCKED), so figures come from the chart PNGs in aras-p/aras-p.hugo (bcn-decode-win-vs2022.png, bcn-decode-win-clang14.png, bcn-decode-mac.png), whose bar labels are printed numbers. Output type may differ per decoder (bcdec has half and float BC6H variants; which was timed is not stated). Repo has not been committed to since 2022-06-23.

name: JPEGDEC (bitbank2)
baseline: TJpgDec (via Bodmer/TJpg_Decoder) and picojpeg (via Bodmer/JPEGDecoder); libjpeg-turbo and stb_image not compared
workload: Decode of one 280x240 baseline JPEG held in memory on an ESP32-S3 (with PSRAM), timed with millis() around the library's decode call, with and without drawing to a TFT; JPEGDEC, Bodmer/TJpg_Decoder, Bodmer/JPEGDecoder and Espressif ESP32_JPEG compared.
claimed_speedup: Decode-only ms from the atomic14 table: Bodmer/JPEGDecoder (picojpeg) 108, Bodmer/TJpg_Decoder (TJpgDec) 55, bitbank2/JPEGDEC 32 (older version, struck through), JPEGDEC new SIMD-enabled version 23, ESP32_JPEG 20. Derived from page data: JPEGDEC is 1.7x faster than TJpgDec (55/32) and 2.4x with the new version (55/23); 3.4x and 4.7x faster than picojpeg (108/32, 108/23). Decode plus draw: TJpg_Decoder 64, JPEGDEC 38 (old) or 29 (new), ESP32_JPEG 37. The JPEGDEC README itself gives only per-MCU timings for its own code (tulips 640x480 test image: Cortex-M7 at 600 MHz 29,592 us full decode, Apple M1 992 us at 1/8 scale) and unquantified claims ('performs better than anything else available', 'cropping function that's faster than JPEGTRAN').
compiler_and_flags: PlatformIO espressif32 / Arduino framework with -Ofast (platformio.ini); GCC version and library versions not pinned.
hardware: ESP32-S3 (esp32-s3-devkitc-1, PSRAM enabled); clock speed not stated
tradeoffs: Baseline JPEG only (grayscale or YCbCr Huffman); progressive files are handled only as DC-only thumbnails (the decoder forces 1/8 scale and decodes the first scan). Aims at no more than 18K of RAM for baseline decode when output goes straight to an LCD (comment in jpeg.inl; README says 20K minimum). Callback design: caller supplies draw function, 2048-pixel internal buffer. Built-in 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 scaling, crop, Exif thumbnail, Floyd-Steinberg dithering; SIMD color conversion on ESP32-S3, Arm NEON and x86 SSE2.
caveats: Evidence is an independent but small one-image, one-run-per-library demo (millis() resolution, no repeats, no stated clock, no pinned compiler or library versions); each library uses its own callback so the work per call is not identical; Espressif's ESP32_JPEG was faster in decode-only (20 vs 23 ms). Comparison against desktop libjpeg-turbo, stb_image and the lead's '1/8-scale progressive in about 18 KB' claim has no published numbers anywhere found. The repo's own wiki (Home page only) has no benchmark; the README chart (perf.jpg) shows only JPEGDEC on different boards. Newest numbers in atomic14's repo are dated 2024-04-07. A search snippet of an esp32.com thread (blocked here) also compares rom tjpgd.h and JPEGDEC but could not be read.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/bitbank2/JPEGDEC (README, jpeg.inl, perf.jpg); WebSearch 'JPEGDEC vs TJpg_Decoder decode time ms comparison issue benchmark ESP32 tjpgd' surfaced github.com/atomic14/esp32-jpeg-perf-tests

name: rusty_webp (remade_ffmpeg_rs crates/rusty_webp)
baseline: libwebp (default lossless effort m4, driven through FFmpeg 8.1.2's libwebp encoder); decode rows are against FFmpeg's native VP8/VP8L decoder, not libwebp
workload: Pinned single-core child CPU time, ABBA-interleaved pairs (N = 21-31, null-arm floor 5% or less), on a real-content corpus (Derf video frames 1080p to 8K, screen captures, alpha, odd sizes): lossless VP8L encode versus libwebp m4, plus lossy and lossless WebP decode versus FFmpeg.
claimed_speedup: Lossless encode: '1.6-2.8x faster than libwebp's default effort (m4)' at '+4...13%' size on photos (smaller than libwebp m0 on every corpus image) and 'up to 39% smaller' than m4 on screen or repeated content. Decode versus FFmpeg: lossy (VP8) 8K '1.24-1.29x faster, bit-exact'; lossless (VP8L) 8K '~2.15x faster'.
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, #![forbid(unsafe_code)], lossless VP8L encode and VP8/VP8L/animated decode, native YUV 4:2:0 output; no lossy (VP8) encoder. The encode speed comes with larger files than libwebp m4 on photographs (+4 to 13%). Lives as one crate in the remade_ffmpeg_rs monorepo (crates/rusty_webp), also published as the rusty_webp crate.
caveats: First-party, and the WebP harness is not in the repo: tools/bench has a generic pinab.py but no WebP script, docs/benchmarks.md covers VP9 only (Intel Core i7-14650HX), crates/rusty_webp/examples holds only decode_bench.rs, and the Derf corpus is not shipped; compiler, flags and CPU for the WebP rows are unstated. The libwebp baseline is reached through FFmpeg's libwebp wrapper, not cwebp. Decode wins are against FFmpeg's decoder; the upstream image-webp README says its decode is 70-100% of libwebp. The fork's NOTICE.md records that the first version was 16-23x faster at encode but produced 35-53% larger files, so the 1.6-2.8x figure is a size/speed trade chosen after tuning. Repository shows AI-assistance (CLAUDE.md, .claude directories); the rusty_webp path has two commits, both 2026-08-12 (repo-wide last commit 2026-10-05). This record shares repo_url with the existing remade_ffmpeg_rs record, so it needs a paper: id (for example paper:rusty-webp) when merged.

name: honeydiff (vizzly-testing)
workload: README 'Performance' snapshots from local benchmark runs on its own Vizzly screenshot fixtures (default and strict/no-AA comparison, tall screenshot) and isolated 1080p SSIM and GMSD; no other library timed.
claimed_speedup: No comparison against odiff, pixelmatch or any other library. Own timings only: Vizzly screenshot default ~2.81ms, strict/no-AA ~2.18ms, tall screenshot default ~147ms, tall strict/no-AA ~4.34ms, 1080p isolated SSIM ~14.7ms, GMSD ~10.9ms. CHANGELOG has self-comparisons only (SSIM 5x faster than the previous release, 239ms to 51ms at 1920x1080).
tradeoffs: Node.js 22+ package with prebuilt native binaries (macOS ARM64, Linux x64/ARM64, Windows x64); CIEDE2000 perceptual threshold, anti-aliasing suppression, region clustering, SSIM/MS-SSIM/GMSD, WCAG contrast and CVD simulation. It is a richer feature set than pixel-count diffing, so it is not a like-for-like comparison with odiff or pixelmatch.
caveats: The public repo holds only the JS loader, type definitions, examples and release metadata; the Rust source is not here (package.json points to vizzly-testing/r-honeydiff, which returns 404), so the MIT licence cannot be exercised on the engine code. README links benchmarks/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md, which also returns 404. 'Current local benchmark snapshots' state no hardware, flags or harness. Web search found no third-party honeydiff benchmark (BlazeDiff, a different tool, claims 4.4-4.9x over odiff). Recorded at tier D as the lead's named rival of odiff despite few stars.

name: zenquant (imazen)
baseline: libimagequant (imagequant crate 4, presets s1 d50, s1 d100, s4 d100); also quantette 0.5 k-means, quantizr, color_quant
workload: 256-colour quantization of 50 images from three corpora (CID22, CLIC 2025, screenshots) with default dithering; scored by butteraugli, SSIMULACRA2, DSSIM, PNG size (zenpng aggressive deflate), GIF size and approximate per-image milliseconds from the multi-threaded default run.
claimed_speedup: Not a speed claim; zenquant's pitch is smaller files and better butteraugli at similar time. README table: zenquant Best butteraugli 3.17, SSIMULACRA2 82.9, DSSIM 0.00058, PNG 586 KB, GIF 764 KB, ~542 ms; imagequant s1 d100 4.10, 82.2, 0.00056, 637 KB, 848 KB, ~546 ms; imagequant s4 d100 4.39, 81.9, 0.00057, 640 KB, 854 KB, ~315 ms; quantette k-means 3.86, 83.9, 0.00050, 616 KB, 799 KB, ~265 ms; zenquant Fast 3.29, 82.6, 0.00069, 582 KB, 749 KB, ~321 ms. Derived from page data: Best PNG is 8% smaller than imagequant s1 d100 at the same ~ms; Fast is 1.7x faster than imagequant s1 d100 (321 vs 546) but no faster than imagequant s4 (315) or quantette (265).
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --example quantizer_comparison --release; runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX2+FMA, NEON, WASM128), no -C target-cpu=native; rustc version not stated
stars_or_usage: crates.io zenquant 0.1.3 (8,680 downloads); default quantizer in zenpng, zengif, zenwebp
tradeoffs: OKLab pipeline with butteraugli-inspired adaptive-quantization masking, median cut, k-means, format-aware palette sort, Floyd-Steinberg and optional Viterbi run optimization; no_std plus alloc, forbid(unsafe_code), SIMD dispatch. AGPL-3.0 network copyleft unless a commercial licence is bought ($1 startup tier); the README says quantette leads on per-pixel metrics and imagequant looks best to the eye.
caveats: Not faster than the incumbents in the README table: zenquant Best takes the same ~542 ms as imagequant s1 and the Fast preset only ties imagequant s4 and loses to quantette. The ~ms column comes from the default multi-threaded run, which the repo's own benchmarks/README.md says is 'fine for the quality columns, not for timing claims'; the single-thread --benchmark mode has no committed result and the cross-library run records no CPU, RAM or compiler. Evidence is first-party and the README notes AI-generated code ('Not all code manually reviewed'). Licence is dual, so the AGPL branch is copyable but with network copyleft.

name: Simd (ermig1979)
baseline: OpenCV (cv::resize and colour conversion) and libyuv; no published comparison found
workload: No published OpenCV or libyuv comparison. The repo has a test mode that times each Simd function's scalar and SIMD implementations against each other, and an optional SIMD_OPENCV build in which ResizeOpenCvSpecialTest times Simd resize against cv::resize on a BGR24 480x640 to 333x444 image, but no numbers are published.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'many useful high performance algorithms for image processing' optimized with SSE, AVX, AVX-512, AMX (x86) and NEON, SVE, SVE2 (Arm). Release notes (docs/2025.html) mention 'Special tests to compare Simd and OpenCV resize' and a SimdResizeMethodBilinearOpenCv mode with AVX2 and AVX-512BW optimizations, with no timings.
stars_or_usage: 2.3k stars; vcpkg port; proposed as an OpenCV replacement in wpilibsuite/allwpilib issue 7108 (no numbers)
tradeoffs: C API with C++ and Python wrappers; broad coverage of pixel format conversion, resize and filtering, statistics, motion and object detection, and neural-network inference (Synet); x86 SSE to AMX and Arm NEON, SVE, SVE2; dynamic or static link, CMake and MSVS; Windows and Linux, 32 and 64 bit.
caveats: Claim-only: the project's benchmark pages live on ermig1979.github.io, which is EGRESS_BLOCKED here (raw.githubusercontent.com/ermig1979/ermig1979.github.io/{HEAD,master,main}/README.md all return 404, so no pages repo was reachable); docs/ in the repo holds release notes per year and the Doxygen help, with no OpenCV or libyuv timing tables. Web searches found no third-party Simd versus OpenCV or libyuv benchmark. Revisit if the blocked pages carry numbers.
